Hide
HīD
v. (rendering Hebrew sāthar, tsāphan, chābā', and Greek kruptō)
From Old English hīdan, to conceal, cognate with Greek keuthō — and unrelated to the other English hide, an animal skin, though both come down from the same distant root idea of covering. The Hebrew has several words with distinct flavours: chābā' is to hide oneself in fear, sāthar is to conceal or be secret (whence the secret place), and tsāphan is to hide by storing up, to treasure — which is the word behind hiding God's word in the heart.

Biblical Definition

Scripture uses hiding in three directions, and they must be kept apart. First, the creature hides from God, which is the immediate reflex of guilt: “Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden” (Gen 3:8). It is futile — the LORD calls, Where art thou? — and every subsequent concealment of sin is a repetition of it, which is why the proverb says that he that covereth his sins shall not prosper, but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. Second, God hides the believer, and this is pure mercy: “Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance” (Psa 32:7) — and it is worth noticing that this is the psalm of confessed sin, so the man who stopped hiding from God found a hiding place in Him. Isaiah gives the same shelter an eschatological form: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers…hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast” (Isa 26:20). Paul states the settled position of the believer in this life: “ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God” (Col 3:3) — hidden, and therefore safe, and therefore not yet visibly what it will be, for when Christ who is our life shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory. Third, the believer hides God's word, storing it as treasure: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

To conceal; in Scripture, the guilty creature's futile concealment from God, God's merciful concealment of His people in Himself, the believer's life hid with Christ in God, and the storing of God's word in the heart as treasure against sin.

expand to see more

HIDE, v.t. 1. To conceal; to withhold or withdraw from sight; to place in any state or position in which the view is intercepted from the object.

2. To conceal from knowledge; to keep secret. Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do? Gen. 18.

3. To protect; to shelter. Thou art my hiding place. Psalm 32. Hide me under the shadow of thy wings. Psalm 17.

4. To treasure up; to lay up in store. Thy word have I hid in mine heart. Psalm 119.

5. To hide the face; when spoken of God, to withdraw the tokens of his favor; when spoken of men, to refuse to look upon, whether in shame or in contempt. Isa. 53; Isa. 59.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:8 — "And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden."

Psalm 32:7 — "Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah."

Colossians 3:3 — "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God."

Psalm 119:11 — "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee."

Modern Corruption

The instinct to hide sin is now assisted by a culture of curated appearance, while the biblical remedy — confession to God and, where fitting, to men — is treated as unnecessary exposure rather than as the way out.

expand to see more

Concealment is the oldest post-fall reflex, and every age gives it new instruments. Adam had leaves and trees; the present age has a managed public self, edited and maintained, in which the gap between the presented life and the actual one can be held open indefinitely. The particular danger is that this feels like privacy rather than like hiding, and privacy is a real and legitimate good. The test is simple and Scripture supplies it: hiding that would be undone by confession is concealment of sin, and concealment of sin does not prosper. Psa 32 is the case history, written by a man who tried it — when I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long — and who found relief only at the point of acknowledgment.

The opposite error deserves naming too, because the reaction against concealment has produced a compulsory openness in which every fault is published and nothing is kept. Scripture does not require this. Confession is directed — to God always, to the one wronged where there is a wrong, to the church where the matter is the church's — and love covereth a multitude of sins. Indiscriminate disclosure often serves the discloser and injures others, and it can coexist quite comfortably with impenitence. What Scripture asks is not exposure but honesty before God, and the promise attached to it is the one Psa 32 gives: blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered — covered, that is, by God, which is the only covering that works.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew distinguishes hiding in fear (chābā'), hiding as secrecy or shelter (sāthar), and hiding as treasuring up (tsāphan). Greek kruptō and its compounds cover concealment, with apokruptō for what God has hidden from the wise and revealed unto babes.

expand to see more

Hebrew chābā' (H2244) — to hide oneself, to withdraw in fear; the word of Adam among the trees and of Saul hidden among the stuff (1Sa 10:22).

Hebrew sāthar (H5641) — to hide, to conceal, to be secret; gives sēther, the secret place of Psa 91:1, and the phrase hide thy face.

Hebrew tsāphan (H6845) — to hide by storing, to treasure up; the verb of Psa 119:11, and of the goodness God has laid up for them that fear Him (Psa 31:19).

Greek kruptō (G2928) — to hide, conceal, keep secret; used of the treasure hid in a field and of the life hid with Christ in God (Col 3:3).

Greek apokruptō (G613) — to hide away, conceal from; used of things hid from the wise and prudent and revealed unto babes (Mat 11:25; Luk 10:21).

Usage

"Of guilty concealment: Adam and his wife hid themselves (Gen 3:8); he that covereth his sins shall not prosper (Pro 28:13)."

"Of divine shelter: thou art my hiding place (Psa 32:7); hide me under the shadow of thy wings (Psa 17:8); hide thyself until the indignation be overpast (Isa 26:20)."

"Of treasure and of present concealment in Christ: thy word have I hid in mine heart (Psa 119:11); your life is hid with Christ in God (Col 3:3)."
